summary:
Cloaking research aims to hide objects or events by controlling electromagnetic or sound waves, with potential applications in optics, communications, imaging, and protection from waves. The first electromagnetic cloak was produced in 2006 using gradient-index metamaterials, helping establish transformation optics, which designs materials to steer waves around a region.

Other approaches include concealing events by changing light’s speed, canceling an object’s scattered waves, and reducing scattering with resonant covers. Researchers at Imperial College London proposed event cloaking in 2010; a later optical experiment concealed a time interval of about 10 picoseconds. Many approaches remain limited, for example to particular frequencies or very small objects.

Acoustic cloaking applies similar principles to sound. A laboratory device demonstrated sonar evasion at frequencies of 40 to 80 kilohertz. The article also describes theoretical proposals to use acoustic materials for improved imaging and to shield structures or coastlines from destructive water waves.
